description: Somos a SYNTRA, uma equipe multidisciplinar com habilidades diversas nas áreas de ciência, tecnologia e saúde. Quatro de nós faz parte do IEEE EMBS Student Branch Chapter, da IEEE, fortalecendo nossa conexão com a comunidade científica. Nosso objetivo é desenvolver soluções inovadoras para o monitoramento da saúde de astronautas, unindo conhecimentos em programação, inteligência artificial, engenharia biomédica e ciências espaciais. Valorizamos a colaboração, a criatividade e a inovação!
summary: SISP (Health & Prevention System) is a health integration and prevention layer for space missions. Its core is written in portable, dependency-free C, so it can connect to the sensors already aboard the spacecraft and already used by the crew, such as heart monitors, blood pressure cuffs, glucometers, thermometers and radiation dosimeters, without replacing any hardware. SISP combines these readings, compares each one with the astronaut's own baseline, and scores the risk across NASA's five Human Research Program hazards. The crew sees the results on a visual dashboard with a 3D body model, practical guidance and step-by-step emergency protocols. History is kept in an onboard SQLite database that works with no link to Earth. SISP uses open NASA data, including real Inspiration4 glucose data (OSDR) and DONKI solar events, which trigger a shelter alert and add to the radiation dose. Next steps are automation through piezoelectric pump integration, radiation protection following IAEA protocols, and mental-health monitoring with neural sensors. This matters because far from Earth, communication is delayed and astronauts are not doctors. Building on what is already on board gives the crew autonomy and catches problems before they become crises.
details:
What it does / how it works. SISP is a health integration and prevention layer for space missions. A portable, dependency-free C11 core (libsisp) takes readings from sensors already aboard the spacecraft (heart monitors, blood pressure cuffs, glucometers, thermometers, radiation dosimeters) or typed in at a daily check-in. It covers six indicators: blood pressure, heart rate, blood glucose, temperature, sleep and mood (PHQ-2). Each reading is compared with clinical reference ranges and with the astronaut's own in-flight baseline. It is then graded N0–N3 and mapped to NASA's five Human Research Program hazards. The crew sees the results on a dashboard with an interactive 3D body, practical actions, trends, and step-by-step emergency protocols for cardiac arrest (CPR adapted to microgravity), muscle injuries and fractures. Self-tests include a camera-based pulse estimate and a psychomotor vigilance test (PVT-B) for fatigue. Real DONKI solar events trigger a shelter alert and add to the radiation dose. A compact flight-surgeon report accounts for the communication delay. History is stored in an onboard SQLite database.

Benefits. The crew gets autonomy when Earth is minutes away, problems are caught early instead of at crisis point, and it builds on existing hardware with no new equipment. It works fully offline.

Intended impact. Support long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars, where real-time medical help is impossible and astronauts are not doctors.

Tools. C11 (libsisp core, CMake, ctest, ASan/UBSan) compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten; SQLite (native and sqlite-wasm with OPFS); TypeScript, React, Vite and Tailwind; Three.js (React Three Fiber) for the 3D body; Recharts; Python for NASA data ingestion; GitHub Actions CI and GitHub Pages. NASA data: OSDR OSD-575 (Inspiration4), DONKI, Curiosity RAD and NASA-STD-3001. AI tools were used only as a consultant and for code autocomplete.

Creativity. A 3D body shows where the risk is. Space weather is tied to personal radiation dose. Each astronaut is compared with their own baseline, not a population average. A single deterministic C core runs on spacecraft hardware and in the browser with identical results (321/321 test cases).

Factors considered. Microgravity physiology (space fever, bone loss, sleep loss), communication delay, offline operation, deterministic and verifiable logic, privacy (data stays on board), accessibility (EN/PT, AA contrast, reduced motion) and safety: it is a decision-support prototype, not a medical device, and gives no medication doses.
